prompt: A decision tree with no max_depth limit reached 100% training accuracy but only 91.2% test accuracy on the breast cancer dataset, while a max_depth=3 tree reached 97.6% train and 93.9% test accuracy. What does this pattern show?
choices: The unrestricted tree is underfitting, since its test accuracy is lower than the shallow tree's train accuracy
The unrestricted tree is overfitting: it memorized noise in the training set, which hurt its ability to generalize
Both trees are equally good; the numbers show no meaningful difference
The shallow tree has data leakage because its train accuracy is lower than the deep tree's

Running the same k-NN classifier (k=5) on the breast cancer dataset with and without StandardScaler produced test accuracies of 0.912 (raw) and 0.956 (scaled). Why does feature scaling matter for k-NN in a way it doesn't for the decision tree or random forest in this module?
choices: k-NN uses Euclidean distance, so a feature measured in the thousands (like mean area) can dominate the distance calculation over a feature in single digits; trees split on individual feature thresholds and never compare magnitudes across features
Scaling only affects regression models, not classifiers like k-NN
Trees always require scaling and k-NN never does, the opposite of what happened here

prompt: On a fraud-style dataset where only 3.5% of examples are the positive class, a DummyClassifier that always predicts "not fraud" scored 96.48% accuracy. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Accuracy is always the most reliable metric to report
The dummy classifier is actually a good fraud detector
On severely imbalanced data, high accuracy can be achieved by a model that never correctly identifies the minority class, which makes accuracy misleading
The dataset must contain a labeling error, since accuracy is unusually high

prompt: A model's ROC-AUC on a test set is exactly 0.5. What does that tell you?
choices: The model is perfectly calibrated
The model correctly classifies 50% of examples at every threshold
The model's ranking of positive vs. negative examples is no better than random guessing
The dataset must be perfectly balanced between classes

prompt: On the fraud-style dataset, a default logistic regression scored ROC-AUC = 0.747 but PR-AUC (average precision) = 0.225, and its recall on the fraud class was only 2.3%. Which metric best exposes that this model is nearly useless for actually catching fraud?
choices: ROC-AUC, because it is always the most trustworthy summary metric regardless of class balance
Accuracy, because it was the highest of all the reported metrics
PR-AUC (and recall), because they are computed relative to the minority class and directly expose how few real fraud cases were caught
The intercept term of the fitted logistic regression

prompt: cross_val_score(rf, X_train, y_train, cv=StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)) returns 5 scores. What does each individual score measure?
choices: Accuracy on the full held-out X_test set, recomputed 5 times with different random seeds
Accuracy on one held-out fold of the training data after fitting on the other 4 folds, repeated so every training example is used for validation exactly once
Training accuracy on the entire training set, unrelated to validation
The combined accuracy of an ensemble formed by averaging all 5 models' predictions together
